applied, abundantly show that it was so under-
stood. Not only was the evidence complete as
to the past application of the money and power of
the Bank to electioneering purposes, but that the
resolutions of the Board of Directors authorized
the same course to be pursued in future.

It being thus established by irreproachable
proof, that the Bank of the United States was con-
verted into a permanent electioneering engine,
it appeared to me that the path of duty which the
Executive Department and the Government ought
to pursue, was not doubtful. As by the terms of
the Bank charter, no officer but the Secretary of
the Treasury could remove the deposits, it seem-
ed to me that this authority ought to be at once
exerted to deprive that great corporation of the
support and countenance of the Government in
such of its funds, and such an exertion of
his power.

In this point of the case the question is presen-
ted, whether the people of the United States are
to govern, through representatives chosen by their
unbiased suffrage, or whether the power and
money of a great corporation, are to be secretly
exerted to influence their judgement, and control
their decisions. It must now be determined
whether the Bank is to have its candidates for
all offices in the country, from the highest to
lowest, or whether candidates on both sides of
political questions shall be brought forward as
heretofore, and supported by the usual means.

At this time the efforts of the Bank to control
public opinion, through the discourses of some
and the fears of others, are equally apparent, and
it is possible more objectionable by an acceleration
of its accommodations more rapid than any emer-
gency requires, and even while it retains specie
to an almost unprecedented amount in its vaults,
it is attempting to produce great embarrassment
in one portion of the community, while through
presses known to have been sustained by its mon-
ey, it attempts by unfounded alarms to create a
panic in all.

Those are the means by which it seems to ex-
pect that it can force restoration of the depos-
its, and as necessary consequence, extort from
Congress renewal of its charter. I am happy
to know that through the good sense of our peo-
ple, the effort to create a panic has hitherto fail-
ed, and that, through the increased accommoda-
tions which the State Banks have been enabled to
afford, no public distress has followed the ex-
cesses of the Bank, and it cannot be doubted that
the exercise of its power and the expenditure of
its money, as well as its efforts to spread ground-
less alarm, will be met and rebuked as they de-
serve.

In my own sphere of duty, I should feel my-
self called on by the facts disclosed to order a
scire facias against the Bank, with view to put
an end to those chartered rights it has so palpably
violated, if not that the charter itself will
expire as soon as decision would probably be
obtained from the court of last resort.

I called the attention of Congress to this sub-
ject in my last annual message and informed them
that such measures were within the reach of
the Secretary of the Treasury had been taken to
enable him to withdraw the deposits. The money
in the Bank of the United States were certainly
safe, but that as his single power might lie inadequate to the object, I recommended the subject

Legal Bulletin.—For the benefit of our legal readers, We give place to-day to the opinion of the Circuit Court of the United States for the District of Columbia, in the case of the United States vs. Watkins. It will be recalled that the defendant was convicted on three indictments of misdemeanors, and sentenced to three months imprisonment on each indictment, and to pay certain fines amounting to three thousand and fifty dollars. Upon these judgments three writs of fieri facias were sued out on the said judgments, 1828, 1829, and duly returned at the next term. And in February, 1850, three writs of c. sa. were sued out on the same judgments, returnable at the next May term, but were not returned by the Marshal at that term, nor was he called upon to return them, and nothing appears upon the record respecting them, until the January term of 1853, when the court being in session, of November term 1852, they were filed in the Clerk's office by the Marshal, endorsed as delivered over to my successor in Office. On the 5th January, 1853, the defendant applied to the Supreme Court of the United States for writ of habeas corpus, and upon that proceeding was discharged from custody, upon the ground that the Marshal had no authority to detain him beyond the return term of the writ—unless he had been committed by the Court at the prayer of the plaintiff, and the U. States not having availed themselves of the full benefit of the judgment and execution by bringing in the defendant at the proper time, he was discharged.—The error in the process, consisted in the failure of the Marshal to bring the defendant into Court at the return of the first c. sa. and of the United States Attorney to pray him in commitment. Immediately upon the discharge of the defendant by the Supreme Court of the United States, for the reasons above stated, he was arrested again upon three new writs of c. sa. issued upon the same judgments, and the main question discussed in the opinion of the Circuit Court, was whether the defendant could be lawfully arrested and held in custody upon the second writs after having been taken and discharged upon the former writs. The Court decided that he could not, upon the long established principle of the common law, that no man shall not be twice taken in execution for the same cause.

interesting changes in the seasons—something, which leads
every reflecting mind to acknowledge
with gratitude the existence of some
supreme power; it is doubtless admitted
that every season has its peculiar
beauties, but to me none has ever
been the most delightful of them all.
Winter is the season for social inter
course, for the enjoyments of the
nestled circle, and the dear delights of
the cheerful residence. Spring comes
fastening onward, now gladdening the
garth with cheering sunbeam, now
refreshing it with a passing shower, all
animal and vegetable creation appears

decked with green carpet, which the

slippers and strews the garth with
flowers, she clothes the forest with its
leafy foliage, while the sweet south
wind comes stealing by, wafting to the
captured senses the most delicious
fragrance; yes these with variety of
others are the beauties of summer.

with it a charm peculiar to itself; to
me it is ever welcome. Hail it as the
harbinger of happy days, as the ava
kener of holy thoughts; greet it with
feelings of delight, as a

absence.

Poor of New Castle county, held at the Poor
House, June 22d, 1888, the following pream-
BILE and resolutions were adopted:


Whereas it has been represented to the |
Trustees of the Poor of New Castle county, |
that passengers and emigrants from foreign
countries, who have landed in this country,
under licences granted to them in pursuance
Of the acts of the General Assembly Of the
State of Delaware, in such case made and
provided, have been interrupted and obstruct-
ed in their passage from this city to the city
of Philadelphia by certain officers and autho-
rites OF the State of Pennsylvania, and have
been threatened with prosecutions for alleged
violations of the health and poor laws of that
state land whereas it appears to the 'Trus-
tees of the Poor of New Castle county, that
emigrants and passengers from foreign coun-
tries, who have landed in this county and
have complied with the laws of Delaware on
thus landing, have full and perfect right to
pass from the State of Delaware into any
other State of the Union, without hindrance
or interruption, or the exaction of any sum
or sums of money for thus passing:


Therefore be it Resolved, that the Tras
tees of the Poor of New Castle county will
save and keep harmless and unidentified, all
foreign passengers and emigrants who have
landed during this present month of June, or
who may hereafter land at any port in the
county of New Castle, and have complied
with the laws of the State of Delaware, in
such case made and provided, as also all cap
tains of vessels, steam boats, and owners of
any kind of conveyance either by land or wa
ter, conveying such passengers and emigrants
who have landed as aforesaid, of and from all
suits, damages and loss occasioned by the
costs of such suits, and of and from all penal
ties for which the said captains, owners. pas
scngcrs and emigrants can be made legally
liable and responsible, under the laws and
regulations of the State of Pennsylvania, or Of
any other State, affecting or concerning said
passengers and emigrants


Resolved, that the Port Physicians of Will
mington and New Castle, the Inspectors OF
the customs, aud other revenue officers at the
said ports, be furnished with copies of the
foregoing resolutions properly authenticated.

merely occupied by Abraham Marlatt,
Hokes Run, on the 1st day of Novem-
ber next; the Court for the second Bat-
talion will be held at the house of William
J. Bosk, in Darkesville, on the 4th of
November. The Regimental Court for
the 9th Regt. will be held at the house of
William Kroesen, in Martinsburg, on the
23d November. Commandants of Com-
panies will report the vacancies in their
respective companies at the Battalion
Courts.


WILLIAM GREGORY, Col.


67th Reg'l. V. Va.
October 11, 1833
